stem: At intake, 15-year-old golfer Odette and her father agreed in writing that he would be told about attendance and that what she says would stay private unless safety was at risk. A month later he calls: "I've been dropping her at the clubhouse every Tuesday. Has she actually been coming in?" Odette has come to two of four sessions. Before each of the others, she texted the consultant that she'd rather hit balls that day. What should the consultant do?
options: Get Odette's permission first, and call him back with the answer
Explain that sessions are private, and suggest that he ask Odette
Tell him that she has come to two of the four sessions so far
Tell him how many she has missed, and what she gave as the reason
rationales: Odette gave her assent to this disclosure at intake, so a second permission isn't needed and only delays an answer he was promised. It would fit if the agreement had left attendance open.
What she says in sessions is private, but his question is about attendance, which the written agreement says he will be told. This would fit if he had asked what she talks about.

Attendance is exactly what Odette and her father agreed he could have, and he has asked for it. Keeping to the terms set during informed consent serves both the guardian's permission and the minor's assent.
The number of missed sessions falls within the agreement, but the reason is something Odette told the consultant, and nothing in it raises a safety concern. The agreement keeps it private.
takeaway: A sharing agreement cuts both ways: give what it promises, and hold what it protects.

stem: Henrik, a collegiate rower, comes to a first meeting at his coach's suggestion. "Coach told us straight out that you don't report to him, so that's fine," he says. "And I know what I want. I rush the first ten strokes of every race. I just can't picture this part. With the physio, I lie on a table and he works on me. Do I just start talking?" What is the best way for the consultant to begin?
options: Explain how sessions work and what each of them will do
Ask what Henrik hopes will be different by season's end
Explain what the coach will and won't hear about the sessions
Reflect how odd it may feel to be sent here by a coach
rationales: Henrik has a goal but no picture of the process or his part in it. Clear, direct information about roles and tasks is what he asked for, and it builds the agreement on tasks that a working alliance needs.
Goals matter early, but he has just named one. Asking again would pass over the question he actually put: what happens in a session?
Reporting lines must be covered during consent, but he raises them only to say he is satisfied. It would be the place to begin if he had wondered what gets back to the coach.
Reflecting feeling would help if he had shown resentment at being sent. He treats the coach's suggestion matter-of-factly; what he lacks is information.
takeaway: Begin with the gap the client shows you; sometimes that is plain information about the process.

stem: Before a fall workshop series, every athlete on a collegiate track and field team fills out an intake form for the consultant. Under "name and pronouns you use," one athlete, listed on the team roster as Rebecca, writes, "Rowan, they/them. I'm telling my teammates and coaches after the indoor season. Right now it's just my roommates and, I guess, you." The first workshop is on Thursday, with the full team and staff. How should the consultant handle names there?
options: Use Rowan and they/them, as the athlete wrote on the form
Open with a round in which everyone gives a name and pronouns
Tell the coaches beforehand that Rowan is the name to use
Use the roster name, and keep Rowan for private conversations
rationales: Using the name and pronouns an athlete gives is usually right, but doing so on Thursday would announce to teammates and coaches something Rowan plans to tell them months from now.
A round can be welcoming when athletes are ready to share. Here it would push Rowan to disclose early or to give a name they don't use, in front of the whole team.
Alerting staff helps when an athlete asks for it. Rowan has told the consultant and means to tell the coaches later, so this would disclose private information.
Rowan's note sets a limit: the consultant knows now, and the team will know after indoors. Following that limit respects confidentiality and leaves the timing of the disclosure with Rowan.
takeaway: The client decides who knows what and when; use a disclosed name as widely as they have asked.

stem: Five professional esports players begin weekly sessions with a consultant. Management will receive a one-page monthly update, and the players wrote the template themselves. When the consultant asks the group how they handle tilt, nobody answers. Then the support player says, "Last split we did one of these. I said I'd choked in the semifinal, and by dinner I had a nickname." Two teammates laugh; the others study their keyboards. What should the consultant do next?
options: Go over what the monthly updates to management will contain
Have the players settle how they'll treat what is said in sessions
Offer individual meetings for what players won't say in a group
Tell a story of the consultant's own tilt, then ask again
rationales: Reporting limits are essential in organizational work, but the players wrote the template. The story is about what teammates did with a disclosure, not what management did.
The support player spoke up and was ridiculed by teammates, so the interpersonal risk lies inside the group. Norms for how members treat what is said are the starting point for psychological safety.
Individual meetings suit topics that are personal to one player. The whole group has gone quiet, and moving talk elsewhere would leave the cause in place.
Modeling can help a group that doesn't know how to begin. These players know how; one of them did it and paid for it, and a story from the consultant doesn't change what teammates do.
takeaway: Find out where the risk of speaking lies before choosing how to lower it.

stem: Marguerite, 52, books a single video session nine days before her first full-distance triathlon, which she says will also be her last. "I don't want a project," she says. "Training has been lovely. It's the wait on the beach that undoes me. My heart pounds, I breathe like a train, and I've burned half my matches before the horn." What should the consultant offer her?
options: A set of mental skills, added one at a time over coming weeks
An assessment to find out which skills need the most attention
One breathing technique to practice between now and the race
A start date after the race, with time to build skills properly
rationales: Skills usually do take weeks to build, and a staged program would suit an athlete with a season ahead. Marguerite has nine days, one session, and no races after this one.
Assessment guides the work when the problem is unclear. She has described when it happens and what her body does, which is enough to choose a simple somatic technique.

Her concern is narrow and physical, and she has nine days for it. A single somatic technique, with an honest word about how much it can do in that time, fits what she asked for and the time available.
Waiting makes sense for an athlete who wants lasting change. This race is her last, so help that begins afterward is no help.
takeaway: Scale the offer to the time and the request; a small, honest offer can be the right one.

stem: A consultant has been contracted to provide voluntary performance support to a fire department; the chief receives attendance totals with no names. Individual meetings happen only if a firefighter asks for one. Opening the twenty-minute kickoff with an engine company, the chief says, "This person's here to figure out which of you is cracking under the pressure," and takes a seat in the front row. Arms fold around the room. What should the consultant do?
options: Tell the crew now what the work involves and what the chief sees
Give the planned talk, and clarify the role in individual meetings
Talk with the chief later about correcting it at the next briefing
Ask the crew what they've heard about the program so far
rationales: The crew has just been told that the program screens them, and they must choose to come back. Correcting the role and reporting lines now, in front of the chief, clears it up for everyone at once.
Individual meetings happen only on request. After that introduction, few are likely to ask, so most would never hear the correction.
Speaking privately with the chief is worthwhile, and would be enough if the crew hadn't heard the remark. Until the next briefing, though, the crew would believe they are being screened.
Asking is useful when the source of a crew's wariness is unknown. Here it is plain, and the question would invite them to repeat the chief's version with the chief looking on.
takeaway: When a third party misdescribes your role to the people you serve, correct it where they heard it.

stem: Before starting with a professional women's soccer club, a consultant turned down the head coach's request for "toughness" reports on players. The coach accepted this, and both signed terms under which individual sessions are private and the consultant has no part in selection. At the first squad meeting, a midfielder says, "Word is you'll be telling them who can handle the big games." Several players nod. What should the consultant do next?
options: Return to the coach to settle what will be reported
Tell the squad what the signed terms say about reporting
Ask the squad what they would be willing to have reported
Follow up with the midfielder in private about her worry
rationales: Settling reporting with the coach is the first move in third-party work, and it has been done. The terms are signed; the players just don't know them.

The question has a settled answer that the squad hasn't heard. Stating the limits of confidentiality and the consultant's role openly, to all who share the worry, is what the Ethics Code asks for at the outset of team work.
Asking players would fit if the terms were still open. Inviting their views on a settled matter suggests that reports are on the table.
A private talk suits a personal concern. Several players nodded, so an answer to one would leave the rest with the rumor.
takeaway: Once reporting terms are set, the people they protect need to hear them.

stem: Linnea, a conservatory pianist, self-referred for "stage nerves." As the consultant describes a biofeedback program, she leans in, tries on the sensor, and asks how soon it shows results. "I can see it working," she says. "What I keep wondering is what I'd be calm for. The audition forms have been on my desk since March. Some days I'd like to find out I don't have to send them." In terms of Bordin's working alliance, what should the consultant do next?
options: Explain more fully how biofeedback would ease her nerves
Offer a different method for easing her nerves on stage
Ask her how comfortable she feels with the consultant
Work out with her what she wants the sessions to achieve
rationales: More rationale strengthens agreement on tasks when a client doubts a method. Linnea expects biofeedback to work; she doubts what it would be in aid of.
A new method would help if she disliked this one. She is curious about the sensor, and any other method would serve the same uncertain goal.
Checking on the bond fits a client who has turned guarded. Linnea is engaged and has just confided something she finds hard to say.
Calming nerves assumes she wants to audition, and she isn't sure that she does. In Bordin's terms the method is acceptable and the goal isn't settled, so agreement on goals comes next.
takeaway: A task the client likes is no use until the goal it serves is agreed.

topic: Preparing for a new sport culture
stem: A consultant who is new to para sport will begin next month with a national wheelchair rugby squad. On a welcome call the captain, Tavita, says, "Ask us whatever you like, nobody here is shy. The only thing is, we've had nine new staff in six years, and we've sat down with every one of them and explained classification from scratch." How should the consultant prepare for the first team meeting?
options: Study the published rules on how players are classified
Plan questions for the players about how classification works
Arrange for the coach to explain how the lineups are built
Develop an opening session on reclassification
rationales: The captain is openly tired of teaching new staff the basics, and the basics are published. Arriving with that homework done shows respect and saves the players' time for what only they can tell.
Curiosity about athletes' experience is valuable, and Tavita welcomes questions. Asking how classification works would make the consultant the tenth newcomer to need the same lesson.
The coach's thinking on lineups may be useful later, but it isn't what the captain raised, and it depends on knowing classification in the first place.
Nothing on the call suggests that players are struggling with reclassification. Planning a session on it before meeting them assumes a need that no one has assessed.
takeaway: Learn on your own what is public; save clients' time for what only they know.

stem: Ximena, an 11-year-old gymnast, comes to a first session with her mother, who has signed the consent forms and explained by phone that Ximena cried at a meet. Ximena stands half behind her, eyes moving from the consultant's desk to a closed cabinet. "Is it going to be like when I got the stitches?" she whispers. What should the consultant do first to begin a relationship with Ximena?
options: Bring out markers and invite her to draw her favorite skill
Ask her mother to tell the two of them about the meet
Tell her in plain words what they will and won't do here
Suggest that her mother sit just outside the open door
rationales: Drawing is a fine way in for a child who has trouble finding words. Ximena has found them: she has asked what will happen to her, and an activity leaves that unanswered.
The mother has already described the meet by phone. Retelling it would turn attention to an upsetting day while Ximena is still worried about this one.
She fears that this will hurt, like an earlier visit. Honest, simple information answers that fear and gives her what she needs in order to assent, which is where trust with a child begins.
Some children talk more easily when a parent sits a little farther off, in view. Ximena is using her mother as shelter, so separating them now would add to her fear.
takeaway: With a worried child, start by answering the question about what is going to happen.

stem: A consultant joins a collegiate men's ice hockey team with open access to practices and road trips. In the first week a veteran explains why the players seem cool: "Last guy was slick. Great slides. After that you never saw him, and when he did come by, he'd check his phone for our names. That was in February." Which approach to the early weeks is most likely to build trust with these players?
options: Give an opening talk on how strong players use mental skills
Be around the rink and the road trips, offering no services yet
Set up short individual meetings to explain what is available
Have the captains tell teammates how the service helped them
rationales: An opening talk can win over players who like the consultant and doubt the content. This team's complaint is about a person who talked well and then wasn't there.
The veteran's story is about absence and not being known. Consultants describe building a connection, often by being present and informal before offering anything, as the base of effective work.
Individual introductions suit players who are curious about services. Booking them now puts the offer ahead of the relationship, much as the last consultant did.
Peer endorsement helps once players have used the service. No one on this team has anything to endorse yet.
takeaway: Presence often earns the trust that services later depend on.

stem: During an intake, professional boxer Bilal mentions that his next camp falls during Ramadan and asks, "Ever worked with somebody fasting through a camp?" The consultant has not. Before there is time to answer, Bilal adds, "Last consultant hadn't either. Went home, read a bunch of articles, and spent the next session telling me what my fast is about." He waits. Which reply is best?
options: "I haven't. Let me read up on it before our next session."
"I haven't. I could connect you with a colleague who has."
"Before I answer, what has you asking about that?"
"I haven't. What should I know about how you do it?"
rationales: Preparing between sessions is often a good sign of respect. It is also the very thing Bilal has just described as having gone wrong.
Offering a colleague would fit if Bilal wanted someone with experience. He faults the last consultant for lecturing him rather than for being new to it.
Asking about the reason for a question helps when it is unclear. Bilal has explained himself and is waiting for a straight answer.

It answers truthfully and treats Bilal as the authority on his own practice. Honesty about limits with an other-oriented, humble stance is what cultural humility looks like, and it is what the last consultant left out.
takeaway: Answer honestly, then let what the client says about past help shape how you learn.

stem: At a ballet company's season-opening reception, the newly hired consultant is introduced to the dancers. Aroha, a soloist, comes over with a plate of food; two colleagues and the artistic director are chatting within earshot. "I read that you do imagery with dancers," she says. "I've always pictured people lying in the dark listening to whales. What is it, really?" What is the best response?
options: Tell her in a sentence or two what imagery involves
Offer a private meeting, and answer then
Suggest a quieter corner of the room before answering
Explain the limits of confidentiality before saying more
rationales: She has asked about the field and disclosed nothing about herself. A short, friendly answer is ordinary public education and a natural start to rapport.
A private meeting is the right offer when a dancer starts describing her own difficulties. Putting off a general question would make the consultant seem guarded for no reason.
Moving away would protect something personal. Nothing personal has been said, and drawing her aside in view of the director might make it look as if something had.
Limits of confidentiality belong at the start of services. Aroha hasn't asked for services, and nothing she said needs protecting.
takeaway: Not every question is a disclosure; a general question can simply be answered.

stem: A technology company's HR director engages a consultant to work with Soraya, a new vice president, on presenting under pressure. In a call, the HR director mentions looking forward to "the session summaries." At a separate get-acquainted meeting, Soraya says how relieved she is that "HR told me it all stays with you. That's just how I want it." No sessions have been held, and nothing is in writing. What should the consultant do next?
options: Draft confidentiality terms, and send them to each for signing
Meet with HR to agree on what the company will receive
Meet with Soraya to agree on her goals for presenting
Meet with both at once to settle what will be shared
rationales: Written terms are needed, but there is nothing yet to write down. The two hold opposite expectations, and a document sent to each would settle by mail what they haven't discussed.
Agreeing with HR alone would add another private version of the terms. Separate conversations are how the two versions came about.
Agreeing on goals is early work with any client, once the terms are settled. Going ahead now would let her speak freely under a promise that HR doesn't share.

Each party has been told something different, and neither knows it. In third-party work the limits of confidentiality are clarified at the outset, and a joint conversation lets both hear the same terms.
takeaway: When parties hold different versions of the terms, get them to one version in one conversation.

stem: Reviewing a stalled case, a supervisor tells a trainee consultant, "Anyone can see that this archer likes you and trusts you. What your notes don't tell me is whether the two of you are after the same result, or whether the archer sees the point of that breathing log you keep assigning." Which framework is the supervisor most likely using to examine the relationship?
options: Rogers's core conditions of a helping relationship
Bordin's model of the working alliance
Jowett's 3+1Cs model of relationships
Ryan and Deci's basic psychological needs
rationales: Rogers's conditions are empathy, congruence, and unconditional positive regard. The supervisor asks about shared aims and the purpose of an assignment, which those conditions don't address.
The supervisor covers a bond (liking and trust), agreement on goals (the same result), and agreement on tasks (the point of the log). Those are the three parts of Bordin's alliance.
Jowett's model, built for coaches and athletes, concerns closeness, commitment, complementarity, and co-orientation. It has no counterpart to seeing the point of an assigned task.
Basic needs are autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Liking and trust touch on relatedness, but shared results and the purpose of a log aren't needs.
takeaway: Working alliance: agreement on goals, agreement on tasks, and a bond.

stem: Devraj, a collegiate esports player, says at the end of a first video session that the consultant "seemed kind of distracted." On the recording, the consultant looks at the camera, nods, and speaks warmly. An excerpt: "My duo's been off since qualifiers," Devraj says. "Kind of cold with me." "And how many hours are you sleeping?" "Six-ish? Anyway, I don't know if she's mad." "Got it. Do you have a warm-up routine?" Which change would most improve the consultant's attending?
options: Look toward the camera for more of the session
Let tone of voice follow what is being said
Stay longer on the topics that Devraj brings up
Give more visible nods and facial responses
rationales: Eye contact is one part of attending and is easily lost on video. The recording shows the consultant looking at the camera.
Vocal qualities carry attention too, and a flat tone would matter. The consultant's voice is warm; it is the questions that miss him.
Twice Devraj brings up his duo partner, and twice the consultant asks about something else. Verbal tracking, staying with the client's topic, is the missing part of attending.
Visible body language helps on a small screen. The consultant is already nodding, yet the next question still leaves his topic behind.
takeaway: Attending includes verbal tracking: warm delivery can't make up for changing the subject.

stem: Aaliyah, a softball player, books a consultant employed by her university's athletic department after seeing a poster in the weight room. "Do you report to Coach?" she asks. "Because if you do, I'm not telling you anything." Under department policy, a coach who refers an athlete is told whether the athlete attended, an athlete may sign a release for a coach to receive a summary of skills covered, and everything else stays private unless safety is at risk. Which answer is accurate for Aaliyah as things stand?
options: "Short of a safety concern, Coach won't hear that you came or what you say."
"Short of a safety concern, Coach will hear that you came but not what you say."
"Short of a safety concern, Coach will hear which skills we cover but not how often you come."
"Short of a safety concern, Coach will hear that you came and what we cover."
rationales: Aaliyah booked on her own and has signed nothing, so neither exception for coaches applies. An accurate statement of the limits of confidentiality is the most useful answer to her question.
Attendance goes to a coach who made the referral. She came because of a poster.
A summary of skills goes to a coach only with the athlete's signed release, and she hasn't signed one.
Both pieces would reach a coach only if the coach had referred her and she had signed a release. Neither is the case.
takeaway: Tell each client how the reporting rules apply to them, not just what the policy says.

topic: Acting on a stated access request
stem: Emeka, an elite swimmer, emails a consultant about race-day focus. "I'm Deaf and I sign," he writes. "Typing is fine for arranging things, but not for talking about racing. An agency called Harborline sent interpreters for my knee surgery consults, and they were excellent. I'm free Thursdays after two." The consultant, who doesn't sign, is open on Thursdays. What should the consultant do next?
options: Ask Emeka how he would prefer to communicate in sessions
Set up text-based sessions, and send him the link
Give him the names of consultants who can sign
Offer to book a Harborline interpreter, and propose a Thursday time
rationales: Asking is the usual first move and would be right if he hadn't said. His email names how he wants to talk, who he has found good, and when, so asking again shows it wasn't read closely.
He is content to type for scheduling and says it won't do for talking about racing. Text sessions would meet the consultant's convenience.
Some clients want a consultant who signs. Emeka chose this one and points to interpreters who have worked well for him.

He has made a clear and reasonable access request. Acting on it, by arranging an interpreter from the agency he trusts at a time he is free, respects his stated preference and removes the work from him.
takeaway: When a client has told you what access they need, arrange it rather than asking again.

stem: A consultant travels with a collegiate women's volleyball team. After the first season, athletes' anonymous comments on the pre-match team meetings are warm. On the rest of the consultant's time on trips, typical comments read: "Getting asked how I was doing at breakfast made me start wondering," and "My Tuesdays on campus cover it. On the road I just want to play." The coaches will support whatever format the consultant proposes. Which travel plan fits best?
options: Hold drop-in hours in the hotel lobby on each evening of a trip
Lead the team meetings, and see individuals only on campus
Reserve a meeting room, and post times for individual sessions
Check in for a few minutes with each athlete on every trip
rationales: Drop-in hours suit athletes who want a quick word and can't find the consultant. These athletes are asking for fewer such contacts on the road.
The team meetings are valued, and the individual contact is unwanted on trips and met at home. Doing less on the road, with that made clear beforehand, fits the feedback.
Booked private sessions would answer a need for longer talks while traveling. Athletes say that their regular campus sessions cover this.
Reaching out to each athlete helps when quiet ones go unnoticed. Here, being asked how they are doing is the thing athletes found unhelpful.
takeaway: Being available isn't the same as being helpful; let feedback set how present to be.

stem: Under a collegiate water polo program's agreement, a consultant keeps individual sessions confidential, has no part in selection, and may facilitate talks between athletes and coaches when both sides want one. Zofia, a junior, has gone to her head coach twice about her minutes; both talks ended in raised voices. Last week the coach told the consultant, "I'd try again if there were somebody in the room to slow us down." Today Zofia says, "I can't do that alone a third time." What should the consultant do?
options: Help her rehearse what she'll say to the coach next time
Pass her concerns to the coach, with her written permission
Offer to arrange a meeting and facilitate it for the two of them
Help her cope with her minutes, and leave the coach out of it
rationales: Rehearsal would build the skills of an athlete who hasn't yet raised the matter. Zofia has tried twice, and what she and the coach both describe is a need for someone in the room.
With a release, a consultant might pass on a fact that a coach needs. Her concerns have reached the coach already; the talks break down when they discuss them.
The agreement allows facilitation when both sides want it, and each has said so. Guiding the conversation, with no voice in selection, stays within the consultant's role.
Working on coping would respect an athlete who has accepted the decision. Zofia still wants to talk with the coach and only says she can't do it alone.
takeaway: Whether to step between athlete and coach depends on the agreed role and on both parties wanting it.

stem: Tendai, a high school basketball player, says, "I miss late, Coach pulls me, and then I'm on the bench with the whole gym looking." "So you miss at the end and then come out of the game," the consultant says. "That's what happened, yeah." Tendai pulls his hood forward until it covers his eyes. "That's not what it's like, though." Which response fits best at this moment?
options: "When you miss late in a game, that's when Coach takes you out."
"You sound ashamed, sitting out there in front of all of them."
"What do you tell yourself at the line late in a game?"
"Being a player they can count on means a lot to you."
rationales: A paraphrase shows that the facts were heard, and the consultant has just given one. Tendai confirms the facts and says they aren't the point.
He hides his face and says the facts leave out what it is like for him. Naming the emotion he is showing, a reflection of feeling, answers that.
An open question about self-talk could start useful work later. It would move him to the free-throw line while he is still on the bench, trying to be understood.
Reflecting meaning fits when a client speaks of what matters to him and why. Tendai is showing a feeling, and nothing he has said is about the kind of player he wants to be.
takeaway: When the facts are understood and the client still isn't, reflect the feeling.

stem: In their fifth session, a consultant urges Aiko, a professional ballet dancer, to trade her usual pre-performance routine for a new one. "I like mine," she says, "but all right." She arrives for the sixth session fifteen minutes late. The new routine, she reports, was "fine." To two questions about it she answers, "You're the expert," looking toward the window. Until now she has done most of the talking. What should the consultant do next?
options: Shorten the new routine so that it suits her better
Ask what has been tiring her out in rehearsals
Go on as planned, and see whether the mood lasts
Own having pushed last time, and ask how that was
rationales: Adjusting the routine would help if she had used it and found it too long. Her replies say little about the routine and a good deal about the relationship.
Outside strain could explain a flat session if she had mentioned any. The change began with her reluctant agreement and shows up when the routine is discussed.
A single off day needn't be examined. Late arrival, minimal answers, and 'You're the expert' just after she was overruled form a withdrawal that waiting would let harden.
She complied against her preference and has since withdrawn. Bringing the rupture into the conversation, beginning with the consultant's own part in it, is how an alliance is repaired.
takeaway: Compliance followed by withdrawal is a rupture; name your part in it and ask.

topic: Protecting psychological safety in a debrief
stem: In preseason, a collegiate women's lacrosse team agreed that mistakes would be discussed without ridicule. Midway through a film session the consultant is leading, a sophomore says she froze on the play that led to a goal. "Shocking," a senior mutters, loudly enough that people laugh. Across the room a freshman, whose hand was half up, lowers it and closes her notebook. There are six clips left to review. What should the consultant do?
options: Point the room back to its own agreement right away
Take the senior aside when the film session is over
Ask others to describe mistakes of their own on that play
Check on the sophomore privately later in the day
rationales: The whole room heard the remark, and the freshman has already decided not to speak. Upholding the team's own norm now, in front of everyone, keeps it safe to own up to mistakes in the clips that remain.
A private word suits something the rest of the room didn't catch. Everyone heard this, and six more clips would go by with the norm broken and no response.
Inviting others to speak can spread the risk in a room that is kind but quiet. In this one it asks players to step into ridicule.
Care for the sophomore is worthwhile, but a later talk with her alone does nothing for the freshman or for the rest of the session.
takeaway: A norm broken in front of the group needs to be upheld in front of the group.

stem: Three weeks ago Dariusz, a professional esports player, decided to be asleep by 1 a.m. to sharpen his reactions. He and the consultant have worked together for a year and speak frankly. "Sleep plan's great, I'm all in," he says cheerfully, then describes a winning streak that had him in ranked matches until 4 on five of the last seven nights. "Anyway," he says, "what's next on our list?" Which response fits best at this moment?
options: "What could you do on nights when you feel like queuing up?"
"You've stuck to a hard change, and it took real discipline."
"You're all in on one o'clock, and you played until four."
"You sound worn down by how hard this has been to keep up."
rationales: Planning helps a client who knows he has a problem to solve. Dariusz thinks the plan is going well, so a question about how to fix it runs ahead of him.
Affirmation would suit a week in which he had kept to the plan. Praising it here would confirm a picture that his own report contradicts.
He states one thing, describes another, and moves on without seeing the gap. Setting the two side by side without judgment is a supportive confrontation, which a strong relationship can bear.
Reflecting weariness would fit if he seemed discouraged. He is cheerful, so this names a feeling he doesn't show.
takeaway: When words and actions diverge unnoticed, place them next to each other and wait.

stem: Sam, a collegiate fencer who uses they/them pronouns, has met with a consultant for months. They once described a coach who got their pronoun wrong: "He was so upset that I spent the rest of practice telling him he was a good person." Today, talking through Sam's last bout, the consultant says "she" for the first time. Sam blinks, then waits to hear the rest of the point. What should the consultant do?
options: Say "sorry, they" and go on describing the point
Leave the bout for now, and ask how that was to hear
Finish the session, and bring it up at the end
Ask what Sam would like done when slips occur
rationales: A short apology and correction owns the mistake without making Sam look after the consultant, which is what went wrong with the coach. Sam is ready for the conversation to go on.
Asking about the impact would be called for if slips had added up or Sam had withdrawn. After one slip, it would make the consultant's mistake the subject of the session again.
Waiting leaves the wrong pronoun standing for the whole session and makes more of it at the end than a correction now would.
Asking for a preference makes sense when the client hasn't shown one. Sam's story shows it clearly enough.
takeaway: Match the repair to the slip and to what the client has shown about repairs.

stem: Brynja, an elite cross-country skier, wants help with her fear of repeating a poor championship. In the second and third sessions, as the talk neared the final climb, she asked about the consultant's own racing days; the consultant answered briefly, and the hour drifted there. Today she gets as far as "So, the climb," stops, and asks, "Did you ever completely fall apart in a big race?" The consultant did, twice. How should the consultant respond?
options: Answer briefly from experience, then bring the talk back to her
Tell her that many elite skiers have had races like that
Ask what she would like to know about the consultant's racing
Say they can come back to that, and stay with the climb
rationales: Brief disclosure with a return to the client is the usual guideline. It is also what was tried twice, and both times it led away from the climb for the rest of the hour.
Normalizing would comfort an athlete who feels alone in this. Here it supplies another way off the subject just as she reaches it.
Curiosity about a first question of this kind might be useful. This is the third at the same moment, and inviting more about the consultant's racing continues the detour.

Each time she nears the climb, a question about the consultant takes them off it. Self-disclosure should serve the client's work, so gently keeping it out and staying with what she began serves her better.
takeaway: Judge a self-disclosure by what it does for the client's work, including what past ones did.

stem: Jun, a 14-year-old tennis player, has spent fifteen animated minutes telling a consultant about a lost match, game by game, and has just reached the three double faults in the tiebreak. Which of two serving drills Jun should take to tomorrow's practice depends on whether the serve routine held up on those points. Jun's mother has pulled into the parking lot. What should the consultant say?
options: "What was the tiebreak like for you out there?"
"Did you go through your routine on those serves?"
"Tell me more about how you were feeling then."
"It sounds like the match slipped away from you."
rationales: An open question gets a reluctant client talking. Jun is already talking freely, and there are only moments left.
One specific fact decides the next step, and the session is nearly over. A closed question gets a particular piece of information quickly.
A prompt for elaboration helps when a story is thin or the feeling needs room. It would open a new topic as Jun's ride arrives.
A reflection would show understanding and might be welcome earlier. It doesn't yield the fact needed to choose the drill.
takeaway: Closed questions earn their place when one specific fact is needed now.

stem: Over fifty minutes of a video session, Captain Otieno, an Army helicopter pilot, has talked about ragged sleep since a rotation began, a new crew member who gets under his skin, and a check ride he is dreading. The consultant now says, "So you're sleeping badly, you're irritated with the new guy, and the check ride fills you with dread. Have I got that right?" Which microskill is the consultant mainly using?
options: Paraphrasing what he has just said
Reflecting the feelings he has shown
Summarizing what he has talked about
Reflecting what his work means to him
rationales: A paraphrase restates one recent statement in fresh words. The consultant reaches back across the session and gathers three separate topics.
Two emotions are named, but as parts of a longer recap that also includes facts about sleep. The purpose is to draw the session together.
Gathering several topics from a stretch of conversation, feelings and facts alike, and checking accuracy is a summary.
Reflecting meaning would bring out the values or significance behind his experience. Nothing is said about why any of this matters to him.
takeaway: A summary gathers content and feeling over time; a paraphrase or reflection takes one piece.

stem: A consultant whose gymnastics career ended after years of competing hurt works with Brielle, a 19-year-old gymnast whose mild back tightness the medical staff is monitoring. Twice the consultant has urged her to "stand up to" her coaches about training load; she looked puzzled, said she likes her coaches, and went on with her imagery. Reading over old notes, the consultant finds the same advice given to two other gymnasts with sore backs. Which reading of the pattern fits best?
options: Countertransference that arises mainly from the consultant
Countertransference that Brielle tends to evoke in others
Transference, with Brielle reacting as if to a past coach
A rupture, with Brielle pulling back from the work
rationales: The advice follows sore backs rather than anything Brielle has asked for, and it matches the consultant's own history. That is countertransference originating in the consultant, a matter for reflection and supervision.
Client-evoked reactions tell you how others may respond to the client too. The consultant had the same reaction with other gymnasts, so Brielle isn't the common factor.
Transference would appear as Brielle relating to the consultant as to someone from her past. The out-of-place reaction here is the consultant's.
A rupture would show in strain or withdrawal on her side. She was puzzled, and she went on with the work.
takeaway: Look at when a reaction recurs: across clients, it points to the consultant.

stem: Lior, a collegiate diver, drops into the usual chair, laughing. "Three weeks, no journal entries. I know. And I'm still hanging on to bad dives, it's driving me nuts. But I sit there with the notebook and nothing comes. I don't think in sentences. Ask me about a dive and I could stand up and show you where it went." In terms of Bordin's working alliance, what should the consultant do next?
options: Talk about how comfortable Lior feels in sessions
Revisit whether quicker recovery is what Lior wants
Set a regular time and place for the journal entries
Try another way for Lior to review missed dives
rationales: Attention to the bond fits a client who has grown guarded. Lior is relaxed enough to laugh about the missed entries.
Reworking the goal would fit if Lior no longer cared about it. Hanging on to bad dives still bothers Lior a great deal.
A set time and place would help someone who means to write and forgets. Lior sits down to write, and nothing comes.
Lior still wants to let go of bad dives, and the writing is what doesn't fit. In Bordin's terms the disagreement is about the task, so change the task and keep the goal.
takeaway: Locate an alliance problem in goals, tasks, or bond before changing anything.

stem: Kalani, an elite wheelchair racer, is deciding whether to race for another four years. "If there were no medals in it," the consultant asks, "what would racing be for?" Kalani starts to speak, stops, and looks down at her gloves. "Hang on," she says slowly. "There's something." Fifteen seconds pass, and she is still looking at the gloves. What should the consultant do?
options: Reflect the feeling that shows in her face
Stay quiet and wait until she goes on
Put the question to her in simpler words
Turn to a topic that's easier
rationales: Reflecting feeling would fit if emotion had welled up and she looked to the consultant. She is searching for a thought, and naming a feeling would interrupt.
She has asked for time and is plainly working something out. Silence is an attending skill, and here the most helpful thing is to do nothing more.
Rewording helps when the question wasn't understood. 'There's something' shows that she understood it and has the start of an answer.
Changing topics would respect a client who didn't want to go there. Kalani has asked the consultant to wait, not to move on.
takeaway: Silence while a client is thinking is work under way; leave it alone.

topic: A small gift at the end of services
stem: After two seasons, Alejandro, a professional cyclist, has met the goals he set with a consultant in private practice, and today is their last scheduled session. On his way out he hands over a jar of quince jam with a card thanking the consultant for "a good two years." He has never given the consultant anything before. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Decline it warmly, and explain the trouble with such gifts
Ask what it means to him before deciding
Accept it with thanks, and leave it at that
Accept it on the employer's behalf, and report it
rationales: Declining is right when a gift is costly or could sway the work. A jar of jam at the close of finished work has no such power, and refusing it could hurt for no reason.
Exploring the meaning helps when gifts recur or come with something the client wants. A single token of thanks at a planned ending explains itself.

The gift is small, offered freely, and tied to a natural ending, so it is neither exploitative nor likely to affect the work. Gracious acceptance respects the client and the Ethics Code's conditions on gifts.
Reporting gifts fits a consultant whose employer requires it. This consultant is in private practice, with no employer to report to.
takeaway: Weigh a gift's value, timing, and pattern; a small closing token can simply be accepted.

stem: On trips, a collegiate field hockey team's players are in their rooms by 10:30 p.m., and the team's agreement with its traveling consultant puts individual meetings between 8 and 8 except in an emergency. At 10:50 one night, Destiny, a junior, taps on the consultant's hotel room door. "I saw your light. I'm fine, just annoyed about getting benched, and I figured you'd be good to vent to." The next match is tomorrow at four. What should the consultant do?
options: Offer her a time to talk tomorrow after breakfast
Talk with her now in a quiet part of the lobby
Walk with her to the athletic trainer on call
Stay with her, and call the team's crisis contact
rationales: She is annoyed, not in distress, and there is a whole morning before the match. Keeping to agreed hours and the team's rule, with a definite time offered, holds the boundary and still meets her need.
A public spot is the right place for a late talk that can't wait. This one can, and going ahead would set aside both the curfew and the agreed hours.
The trainer is the right contact for a physical complaint. She describes none.
Staying and calling for help is required when someone may be at risk. Nothing she says or does suggests it.
takeaway: Hold agreed hours for ordinary upset, and break them for risk.

topic: Client invitation to a public event
stem: A consultant has worked for five years in a university athletic department, with an office beside the pool, and sees many of the swimmers individually. Each year on Senior Day the whole support staff lines the deck and shakes hands with the graduating swimmers as they are introduced. Riley, a senior and a regular client who often tells teammates about their sessions, stops by the office and asks, "You'll be out there Saturday, right?" What is the most appropriate response?
options: Decline, and mark the milestone with Riley in a session
Say yes, and take part along with the rest of the staff
Ask how Riley wants to handle being seen together
Suggest that Riley check with the head coach about it
rationales: Marking a milestone in session suits a personal invitation, such as a family party. This is a work event where the consultant has an ordinary staff role.
Standing with the other staff is part of the job, singles out no one, and reveals nothing about who is a client. Not every contact outside sessions is a multiple relationship.
Planning for being seen together protects a client when the contact would reveal the relationship. A handshake that every senior gets reveals nothing, and Riley talks about the sessions openly.
The coach's approval would matter for someone who had no standing place at the event. The support staff attends each year.
takeaway: Ask what role you'd hold at an event: a staff role differs from a personal one.

topic: Conflict of interest in a small community
stem: A consultant in a town of six thousand gets a call from the parents of Ethan, a 16-year-old club pitcher. "He's fighting one other boy for the last spot in the rotation, and it's eating him up," his mother says. "We thought of you because you know everybody." The consultant does know the other boy: he is upstairs doing his homework, and he will want dinner soon. What should the consultant do?
options: Take the case, with regular consultation from a colleague
Take the case, after agreeing on how to handle chance meetings
Meet with Ethan first, to hear whether he wants the help
Turn down the case, and give them names of other consultants
rationales: Consultation with a colleague supports a consultant who is competent and new to some part of a case. It can't remove a parent's stake in the rival's success.
A plan for chance meetings manages the light overlap that small towns bring, such as sharing a church. Here the consultant's own child gains if Ethan loses out.
A minor's assent matters in any case that can be accepted. Meeting Ethan would begin a relationship that the consultant shouldn't enter.

The rival is the consultant's own child. Wanting one's child to win a spot that the client also wants is a multiple relationship likely to impair objectivity, so it is better to decline and point the family elsewhere.
takeaway: Some small-town overlap can be managed; a stake in the outcome calls for declining.

stem: At intake, Noor, a 26-year-old professional squash player, agreed that texts with the consultant are for scheduling and that other matters wait for sessions. She has kept to this for two months. At 11:40 on Saturday night, after a tournament loss, she texts, "Lost to her AGAIN. Why do I rush the third game every time?? Anyway. Drowning my sorrows in noodles." Their next session is on Tuesday. What should the consultant do?
options: Raise the growing reliance on texts in Tuesday's session
Call her tonight, and follow the safety steps set at intake
Reply on Monday that they can take it up on Tuesday
Suggest on Tuesday that she see a counselor
rationales: Exploring reliance in session suits a run of late-night messages. One text in two months is a slip after a hard loss, and treating it as a pattern would be out of proportion.
A call and safety steps are needed when a message hints at risk. Frustration about a third game, followed by noodles, doesn't.
A brief reply in working hours that moves the topic to the session keeps the agreed boundary, acknowledges her, and makes no more of it than it is.
Suggesting a counselor would follow signs of a clinical concern. Disappointment after a loss is ordinary, and it is a performance topic that belongs in their sessions.
takeaway: Answer a single slip with a light, consistent return to the agreement.

stem: Folake, a professional surfer and current client, wins her first major event and posts, "Couldn't have done it without my mental performance coach!" with the consultant's name. She is now on a long flight home. A sports reporter phones: "She's told the world already, so I just need a line from you. How long have you two worked together?" Folake has signed no release. What should the consultant do?
options: Confirm that she is a client, and say nothing more
Describe in general terms how the consultant trains surfers
Give a short comment that Folake can approve before it runs
Explain that the practice doesn't discuss who its clients are
rationales: A bare confirmation would be acceptable if Folake had released that much. Her own post is hers to make; it doesn't free the consultant to confirm the relationship.
General education suits a reporter writing about mental training. In answer to a question about Folake, a description of work with surfers would all but confirm it.
Approval after the fact comes too late: in giving the comment, the consultant would already have discussed a client with a reporter.
Confidentiality belongs to the client, and only she can release it. A standard reply that neither confirms nor denies protects her until she decides, and it is the same one any client would get.
takeaway: A client's public post doesn't waive the consultant's duty of confidentiality.

topic: One-on-one with a minor while traveling
stem: Zdenek, 15, wrestles for a club covered by the Minor Athlete Abuse Prevention Policies. At a national championship, an hour before his semifinal, he approaches the club's consultant. "Can I ask you about something? I don't want the guys hearing it. Or the coaches." The team is camped out in a block of seats above the mats, and his parents, who have approved his meetings with the consultant, won't arrive until evening. Where should the two of them talk?
options: In the team's block of seats, among teammates
On an empty row across the aisle, in view of the team
In the warm-up room, with an assistant coach beside them
On a video call that evening, with a parent in the next room
rationales: Talking among teammates is observable, and it would do for a quick reminder. It puts his teammates in earshot, which he has asked to avoid.
Others can see and interrupt, so the one-on-one policy is met, and they can't overhear. It protects him and his privacy, and it happens before he wrestles.
A second adult beside them meets the policy and would suit an athlete who wanted the coach there. He has asked that coaches not hear.
A call with a parent close by can meet the policy for electronic communication. It would come hours after the semifinal that he faces within the hour.
takeaway: Observable and interruptible doesn't have to mean overheard.
